name: AutoMOOSE
inputs: Natural-language phase-field simulation request; MOOSE installation with a registered physics plugin (grain growth or spinodal decomposition); LLM endpoint (Claude API or self-hosted OpenAI-compatible model); local or HPC compute
outputs: Generated MOOSE input files, executed simulations, screening and physics-falsification verdicts, kinetics analyses, visualizations, and provenance/recovery records
notes: Six-agent framework (Architect, Input Writer, Runner, Reviewer, Visualization, physics-grounded Skeptic) from University of Illinois Chicago and Argonne's Center for Nanoscale Materials. On a prospectively specified 25-task copper grain-growth benchmark it wrote valid inputs for all 25 tasks, 19 runs showed measurable coarsening, and 15 passed Burke-Turnbull kinetics and Skeptic falsification; a conserved Fe-Cr spinodal case is also shown. Automatic recovery changes only numerical settings, stops after three attempts, and asks the user to confirm unknown or low-confidence failures; repaired runs must pass the Skeptic again. In-silico only. Distinct from the existing MooseAgent and MOOSE-Chem records.

name: OpenAI4S
domain: Code-as-action computational research across chemistry, biology and materials science
inputs: Natural-language research requests, user data, bundled code skills, public-database connectors and a chosen model provider
outputs: Executed Python/R analyses, versioned artifacts, action ledgers, reports and resumable research sessions
notes: Research agent from Peking University Shenzhen Graduate School (PKU-YuanGroup) with Beijing Yuankong Intelligent Technology; the README credits the Peking University-YuanKong Intelligence AI Joint Research Laboratory. The name stands for 'Open AI for Scientist' and does not denote an OpenAI product; the README presents it as an open-source reproduction of the Claude Science architecture. Structured tool calls handle orchestration and permissions while scientific actions run as code cells in persistent Python and R kernels, with an append-only action ledger, versioned artifacts and checkpoints. MIT. The paper scores 36 computational scenarios in chemistry, biology and materials science with an author-built evaluator. Gated operations use a permission broker; in keyword-triggered biosecurity screening only BLOCK stops execution, while ESCALATE is advisory and does not wait for a human decision. No laboratory loop is demonstrated.

name: AutoResearchClaw
domain: Idea-to-paper autonomous computational research with optional human co-piloting
inputs: A research idea or topic, model/agent backend configuration and local compute (GPU/MPS/CPU) with a Docker sandbox
outputs: Literature-grounded hypotheses, sandboxed experiment code and results, verified citations and a LaTeX paper draft
notes: AIMING Lab (UNC-Chapel Hill) 23-stage pipeline: multi-agent debate for hypotheses and result analysis, a self-healing executor with a Pivot/Refine loop, checks of reported numbers and citations against executed outputs, and lessons carried across runs. MIT. Three gate stages wait for human approval unless auto-approve is set. In the paper, Full-Auto runs completed idea-to-paper on 8 of 10 topics, but targeted human input at key stages scored higher than full autonomy. The main benchmark is 25 ML topics, with a smaller extension in high-energy physics, systems biology and statistics. All experiments are computational. Distinct from AutoResearch (EvoMap), Karpathy's autoresearch and ResearchClawBench.

name: data-to-paper
domain: Autonomous data-driven research with backward-traceable manuscripts
inputs: Annotated datasets, an optional research goal and LLM API access; optional human co-pilot review
outputs: Research goals and hypotheses, analysis plans, debugged analysis code, tables, literature citations and complete manuscripts whose numbers are traced back to code and data
notes: Technion Kishony-lab platform that guides interacting LLM and rule-based agents through 17 predefined research steps, from annotated data via literature search (Semantic Scholar), hypothesis and analysis code to a manuscript whose numeric results are programmatically chained to code and data. Published in NEJM AI (2025); MIT. In the reported autopilot runs a user approved each research step (overseeing only). For simple goals the authors report manuscripts recapitulating peer-reviewed results without major errors in about 80-90% of runs; human co-piloting becomes critical as goal complexity increases. Statistical analysis of supplied data only; no new experiments are run.

name: ASI-Arch
aliases: AlphaGo Moment for Model Architecture Discovery
inputs: An architecture research target, seed architecture and baseline, a user-supplied training/evaluation script, LLM API access, GPU compute, and the database and cognition-base services
outputs: Proposed and implemented architectures, training and benchmark results, analyses and an experiment database
notes: GAIR-NLP multi-agent loop (Researcher, Engineer, Analyzer, experience repository) that proposes, implements, trains and analyses linear-attention architectures, using an experiment database and a cognition base distilled from about 100 papers. The paper reports 1,773 autonomous experiments at 20M parameters; the authors then selected about 150 candidates for 340M verification (105 state-of-the-art; the repository lists 106) and 5 for 1.3B validation. The Apache-2.0 release includes the pipeline, both services and the discovered architectures; the training script must be supplied by the user. Closure is computational and GPU-intensive. Separate system from the later GAIR-NLP ASI-Evolve. The repository keeps the v1 title 'AlphaGo Moment for Model Architecture Discovery'; the current arXiv title is 'Neural Architecture Discovery via Autonomous Evolution'.

name: OpenEvolve
domain: Open evolutionary coding agent for program, algorithm and mathematical discovery
inputs: An initial program, an evaluator that scores candidates, and LLM backend configuration
outputs: Evolved programs and their evaluation scores across iterations
notes: Evolutionary coding agent created by Asankhaya Sharma (GitHub codelion), now hosted by the Algorithmic SuperIntelligence Labs organisation and described in its repository as an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve. Apache-2.0. An LLM ensemble proposes code changes, a user-supplied evaluator scores them, and a MAP-Elites program database with islands decides which programs are kept. It is an independent reimplementation and is separate from Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve. No primary paper was found; the README asks users to cite it as software. Papers from 2026 use it as a baseline or search harness for discovery agents. Independent groups have applied it to combinatorial bijection construction and to Zarankiewicz-number bounds. The user defines the problem, initial program and evaluator. The loop then closes computationally, with no physical loop.

name: ARK (idea2paper.org)
domain: Idea-to-paper research automation with computational experiments; example outputs in machine-learning and systems research

paper_links.label: ICML 2026 AI for Science workshop poster

inputs: A research idea or proposal PDF, a target venue template, user-supplied model API keys, and local, Slurm or SkyPilot cloud compute
outputs: Literature survey, experiment code and results, venue-formatted LaTeX paper and iterative AI review reports
notes: Multi-agent idea-to-paper system from SANDS Lab, KAUST (repository kaust-ark/ARK, service at idea2paper.org). Agents for research, planning, coding, experiments, writing and review take a project from proposal analysis and literature search through local, Slurm or SkyPilot cloud experiments to a venue-formatted LaTeX paper; an AI reviewer scores each draft and the revision loop repeats until a score threshold. Apache-2.0 and self-hostable; the hosted instance runs on the user's own model API keys. Before risky actions such as deletions, cloud provisioning or crossing a spend cap it can ask for Telegram approval, but with no Telegram configured it auto-allows and logs them; an ethics-and-soundness gate screens ideas before launch. Described in an ICML 2026 AI for Science workshop poster. Example outputs are ML and systems papers; a study co-authored by one ARK developer also ran it on five ResearchClawBench tasks in neuroscience, energy, life science and physics. Not the same system as AgentAlphaAGI's Idea2Paper (Idea2Story).

name: ScienceBuddy
domain: Interactive biomedical research workspace with self-improving agent harness and model
inputs: Researcher questions with papers, tables, biological sequences or scientific images
outputs: Evidence tables, study plans, presentations and other generated files, with inspectable tool and code-execution trajectories
notes: PhAI Labs hosted workspace in which a ReAct-style agent with 224 mostly biomedical tools plans, retrieves literature and database records, and runs Python, R or Bash code; researchers direct and refine the work in conversation and can inspect each tool call. The paper couples harness evolution with GRPO model training ('recursive-in-recursive self-improvement'); in the reported runs an external frontier model proposes harness edits and user feedback is simulated, on LAB-Bench and Biomni-Eval1 tasks. Workspace case studies are qualitative, translated recordings. The public MIT repository contains only a simplified agent (Simple-SciBuddy) and the self-improvement experiment code; the hosted product source is excluded and hosted-preview access terms are not stated.

name: Quailbot
domain: Agentic scanning tunneling microscopy and instrument operation
inputs: Instrument workspace definitions, CLI instrument drivers and natural-language task prompts
outputs: Instrument actions with linked readbacks, experiment logs, agent completion reports and measurement-ready STM tips
notes: Boston College harness, released as an ISC-licensed Pi extension, that places frontier LLMs inside an STM feedback loop by returning linked readbacks after every instrument action. After a human apprenticeship, launch-prompt-only runs with two frontier models conditioned tungsten tips on FeTe at 4 K to lattice-resolving endpoints without further human messages; a human STM expert verified endpoints afterwards. Disclosed gates: state-changing tools are denied unless the operator enables them with a launch-time environment flag, and piezo-voltage control was withheld for safety. A bent tip, a hidden walker jam and an exhausted sample area needed human disclosure or physical intervention. The demonstrated task is tip conditioning, not a full scientific campaign; workspaces, prompts, transcripts and STM data are promised on Zenodo upon publication.

name: Solver Agent
domain: Agentic calculations and proofs in mathematics and theoretical physics
inputs: Researcher-posed problems in mathematics or theoretical physics; an LLM provider API key (OpenAI by default) and MongoDB; optional Wolfram Engine, CYTools and C++ compiler
outputs: Append-only ledgers of assumptions, derivations, code, outputs and verifier verdicts; answers released after LLM full-solution review; exportable HTML, LaTeX and JSON session records
notes: AGPL-3.0-or-later system by Eliott Morgensztern. A coordinating solver delegates to symbolic and numerical sub-agents, with optional Calabi-Yau (CYTools) and web-literature sub-agents, and logs every step in an append-only ledger; separate LLM verifier agents must accept the full solution before an answer is released. The accompanying paper applies it to global F-theory uplifts of O3-planes and S-folds. The researchers wrote and sometimes split each prompt; one session derived the conditions for Theorem 4.2 without follow-up input. Verification is LLM-based and gives no formal proof-assistant certificate. Requires a paid LLM API.

name: LaMET-Agent
domain: Lattice QCD large-momentum effective theory (LaMET) analysis
inputs: Lattice correlator data (HDF5 with JSON descriptors) and a JSON/JSONC analysis manifest declaring the stage job graph, optionally completed through an LLM planning dialogue
outputs: Light-cone parton distribution functions and distribution amplitudes as NetCDF artifacts, with fit diagnostics, plots, per-stage reports and a final literature-grounded review report
notes: MIT-licensed Python framework that runs a LaMET lattice-QCD analysis as a manifest-declared job graph: correlator analysis, renormalization, Fourier transform, perturbative matching, continuum/pion-mass/infinite-momentum extrapolation, and review. All numerics run in deterministic tools. The LLM is used at three points: an optional planning dialogue that ends with explicit user acceptance of the manifest, bounded and validated choices of fit windows and ranges inside stages, and a final review against the literature that leaves results unchanged. The authors report four end-to-end reproductions (pion PDFs in gauge-invariant and Coulomb-gauge formulations, pion and kaon distribution amplitudes) consistent with published calculations; comparisons across LLM providers, against expert baselines and across repeated runs are still open. Works with a logged-in Codex CLI or with OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek or OpenAI-compatible APIs. The release covers collinear quark distributions; example data come from a separate password-protected host with a self-signed certificate.

name: QIQCBench / Quantum-Harbor
domain: Verified autonomy of AI agents in quantum engineering (simulated hardware)
inputs: Agent harnesses (e.g., Codex CLI, Claude Code, OpenCode) and containerized task bundles with public device specifications and lab notebooks
outputs: Pass/fail verdicts and Elo racing ratings per task and agentic system, graded against logged experiment evidence
notes: Benchmark of 49 expert-authored quantum-engineering tasks run in Quantum-Harbor, a Harbor-based virtual laboratory where agents reach simulated devices with hidden parameters through MCP tools and a separate verifier grades submissions against the logged experiment evidence. The paper evaluates 17 agentic systems. The MIT repository, published by the authors under GaugeForge (a co-author affiliation), releases the framework and five task bundles; the other 44 tasks are not public, so the reported results cannot be fully reproduced. All released tasks run on simulators; the code has an opt-in IBM Quantum live backend, but no hardware run is reported.

name: AstroGenesis
domain: Multi-agent astrophysics research platform (blazars; multiwavelength and multimessenger data, SED modelling)
inputs: Natural-language astrophysics research questions about a source; optionally user-uploaded data files or documents
outputs: Literature syntheses with cited references, retrieved multiwavelength light curves and SEDs (plots, CSV), surrogate-based broadband model fits with best-fit parameters, and up to five ranked candidate research directions
notes: Hosted beta platform (free tier of 10 messages per day; paid Pro tier) from an ICRANet-Armenia-led team with international co-authors. A Supervisor Agent and a Planner/Replanner route each query through literature, data-retrieval, theoretical-modelling and research-ideation agents; the current module covers blazars only. The modelling agent fits SSC, EIC, hadronic and lepto-hadronic models with pretrained neural-network surrogates and Bayesian inference. Only literature retrieval is benchmarked (Hit@5 76.6% single-paper, 79.2% multi-paper); modelling and ideation are shown as worked examples. Runs are user-initiated per query. No source-code release was found.

name: SimuVerity
domain: Engineering-grade Simulink model generation by agents
inputs: 101 natural-language engineering specifications with delivery requirements, solved through MATLAB/Simulink MCP tools; evaluator-owned native simulation scenarios
outputs: Hierarchical scores for delivery, executability, engineering qualification and six quality dimensions
notes: Benchmark from Xi'an Jiaotong University: 101 text-to-Simulink tasks across ten engineering domains, scored by a hierarchical evaluator that runs native simulation scenarios. Six agent systems were evaluated in isolated sessions; the best overall score was 42.86. First-party code and result tables are Apache-2.0. Most bundled reference models are third-party assets under their own terms, some restricted to use with MathWorks products. Generating and evaluating candidates requires proprietary MATLAB R2025a and Simulink. Evaluation is computational simulation only.

name: Ansatz (mathematical research)
domain: Long-horizon mathematical research with continual graph memory
inputs: Mathematical research problems, operator-chosen worker roles and stop conditions, and optional cross-project research memory
outputs: Model-verifier-accepted proof records, exploration graphs, progress reports and research manuscripts
notes: Apache-2.0 release from UCLA (uclanlp), linked from the paper. It extends the Danus architecture (parallel proof workers, a separate verifier, a shared fact graph), and the LICENSE keeps the FrenzyMath copyright notice. A main agent coordinates workers, the verifier and a memory curator over a dependency-linked fact graph and an exploration graph, with optional cross-problem recall. A human operator supplies the problem and sets worker roles and stop conditions; live runs need an authenticated Claude Code CLI and a Codex backend. Acceptance is by model-based review only, with no proof-assistant certificate or independent expert grading. The paper reports 10/10 closures on First Proof Second Batch; the release notes record 9/10 in the archived run and one task resumed after a manual architecture switch.

name: QED (open-problem proof agent)
domain: Natural-language proof generation for research-level mathematical problems
inputs: LaTeX statements of research-level mathematical problems; Codex, Claude or Gemini CLI backends configured per agent role
outputs: Literature-survey notes, YAML proof plans, candidate proofs, structural and detailed verification reports, final natural-language proofs with citations and a proof-effort summary
notes: MIT-licensed pipeline from authors at UC San Diego, Caltech and AWS (work done outside Amazon). It runs a survey agent, a proof-plan decomposer, a prover, structural and detailed verifiers and a regulator that revises the proof, revises the plan or restarts. Codex is the default backend; Claude or Gemini can be set per role. The paper reports 18 open problems contributed by collaborating mathematicians; on five projects, run without human guidance, those experts judged QED's proofs correct and original (probability, algebraic geometry, fluid PDEs, inverse problems). Optional human steering exists but was not used. Checking is done by language models, not a proof assistant, so outputs need expert review.

name: GW-Eyes
inputs: GW posterior samples and skymaps (e.g. GWTC-4.0), EM event catalogs, GCN circulars, and natural-language task requests
outputs: Candidate GW-EM counterpart lists with reports, updated local event database, skymap and luminosity-distance visualizations, and logged tool-call reasoning traces
notes: Peking University LLM agent framework with two sub-agents. The Collector pulls GCN circulars and catalogs, extracts event properties and applies rule-based and self-consistency checks. The Executor plans and runs MCP-integrated tools for GW-EM association, in both directions (GW to EM and EM to GW), plus skymap visualization and rapid verification. Tasks are human-initiated. It was evaluated on simulated injections (50 GWTC-4.0 events) and applied to AGN flares (AGNFRC) and GWTC-4.0, with the associations manually cross-checked. Published in The Innovation (2026). Requires a user-supplied LLM API. MIT-licensed. Distinct from GWAgent.

name: SimulCost
domain: Cost-aware LLM-agent parameter tuning for physics simulations
inputs: Simulation tasks (2,643 single-round, 2,304 multi-round) naming a solver, a tunable parameter and an accuracy requirement; multi-round mode allows up to 10 simulator calls
outputs: Proposed parameter values with convergence and cost feedback traces, scored for success rate and computational cost against brute-force scanning and Bayesian-optimization baselines
notes: Benchmark from the Rose-STL-Lab group at UC San Diego. LLMs tune solver parameters for 12 simulators across fluid dynamics, heat transfer, solid mechanics and plasma physics. In single-round mode the model makes one guess. In multi-round mode it works by trial and error over up to 10 simulator calls, with convergence and cost feedback after each call. Cost is counted analytically for 11 simulators; the production plasma code EPOCH is timed by wall clock and reported separately. The benchmark harness and Hugging Face dataset are Apache-2.0. The required solver library (the first author's simulcost-tools submodule) has no licence file. According to the v4 arXiv comment, CGYRO was removed because of a bug and will be added back. All evaluation is computational simulation.

access_evidence.software_license: Apache-2.0 benchmark harness (Rose-STL-Lab/SimulCost-Bench) and Hugging Face dataset; required solver submodule Eydcao/simulcost-tools has no licence file at verification (2026-10-10), nor do its nested fem_transient_utils and CSMPM_BOW submodules; bundled third-party EPOCH is GPL-3.0

name: HEPLocalAgent
domain: Local natural-language construction and execution of collider simulation workflows
inputs: Plain-language collider simulation requests; a user-selected local language model served through Ollama and a routing profile
outputs: Validated MadGraph, Pythia8 and Delphes inputs presented for expert approval; after approval, locally executed simulation runs with output checks and a JSON run record (commands, cross section, return code)
notes: MIT-licensed local interface from the Indian Institute of Science (Aadarsh Singh, Sudhir K. Vempati). A locally served model proposes a typed workflow; deterministic code restores recognized user-stated quantities, builds and validates inputs for MadGraph5_aMC@NLO, Pythia8, Delphes and a restricted MadAnalysis 5 plan, with a bounded repair loop. Every workflow passes a human approval gate before execution. In the paper, 4 of 7 approved workflows ran to completion, and natural-language routing to MadAnalysis was not demonstrated. The authors describe v1.0.1 as a validation-gated workflow constructor that needs expert approval, not an autonomous agent. External HEP tools keep their own licences.

name: ADMET-EvO
aliases: ADMET-EvO: a self-evolving scientific agent for sustained research across heterogeneous tasks
domain: Self-evolving ADMET and toxicity prediction research for small molecules
inputs: ADMET endpoint definitions, TDC benchmark training/validation splits and optionally curated external assay data
outputs: Hypothesis-tagged experiment ledgers, frozen model configurations, multi-seed test scores and endpoint-specific predictors
notes: Authors are affiliated with Valhalla Technology, CUHK, Zhejiang University and Stanford University. A language-model planning policy proposes falsifiable hypotheses and picks data, feature or model interventions; a separate deterministic evaluator and update rule assign supported, rejected or inconclusive verdicts. The paper reports 22 TDC ADMET tasks and an expansion to 43 toxicity tasks, listed in the repository's Table S2 as ToxCast endpoints. The MIT-licensed repository (v0.3.0) uses a local rule-based planner by default with an optional OpenAI-compatible LLM planner, and external data enter training only after recorded scientific review. All closure is computational; no laboratory validation is reported.

name: SolutionsX
aliases: SolutionsX: supergravity theories/solutions as code, with an agentic workflow for machine-verifiable physics
domain: Machine-verifiable supergravity and tensor-geometry records with an agent toolkit
inputs: A published paper or theory specification, an xAct/Mathematica environment, the curated entry corpus and the shell toolkit with its persistent kernel, method and trap notes
outputs: Replayable machine-verifiable entries (record plus inputs-only evaluation notebook), fresh-kernel verification transcripts, session and progress logs, and a stall report when the ladder is triggered
notes: Single-author Wolfram Language paclet (Vasil Dimitrov, INRNE, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences) built on xAct that stores a supergravity theory or solution as code which replays in a fresh kernel and carries its own verification. Code is AGPL-3.0-or-later (versions up to 2.0.0 were MIT) and the bundled corpora are CC BY 4.0; version 2.1.0 is on GitHub and in the Wolfram Paclet Repository, but the agent toolkit ships only with the GitHub repository. The experimental agent/ toolkit, for shell-capable agents on macOS or Linux, gives an external coding agent a persistent kernel with enforced time budgets and restart-and-replay recovery, a reporter that re-runs a script on a fresh kernel, symptom-keyed method and trap notes, and an advisory stall ladder that tells the agent when to stop and write a report. In three reported runs driven through Claude Code, the agent built 3d Einstein-AdS gravity and the BTZ solution from scratch, then recreated two sections of a published paper on accelerating AdS4 black holes; runs 1 and 2 together took under three hours, and the five authored entries, each replayed on a fresh kernel, are published under Data/Vasko-bot/. The human gave three task prompts and two interruptions, one of them a coordinate-change hint the paper credits with the largest speed-up, and runs the resulting notebook. Limits: the package itself is computer-algebra infrastructure, the model behind the runs is not stated, Claude Code also wrote the toolkit and most of the paper's agent section, and run journals and resource ledgers are available only on request.

name: SPARC (scanning probe agentic research cycle)
aliases: Human-agent discovery of reconfigurable in-plane ferroelectric superdomain control
domain: Agentic scanning-probe microscopy of ferroelectric superdomain control
inputs: A campaign target, piezoresponse microscopy data, instrument-control tools, and the persistent FINDINGS.md and PITFALLS.md memory files with their compiled preflight checks
outputs: Agent-designed pulse-lattice write programs executed on the microscope, graded findings and failure records, per-iteration measurements, and reconfigured in-plane superdomain patterns
notes: University of Tennessee and Rice team (Liu, Slautin, Lin, Kim, Martin, Kalinin) pairing a coding agent, Claude Opus 4.1 in Claude Code on the instrument computer, with one piezoresponse microscope, one shared notebook, and two persistent memory files: FINDINGS.md for graded conclusions and PITFALLS.md for learned failure modes, with selected pitfalls compiled into checks that refuse a design before any voltage reaches the tip. In the operator-controlled Campaign 1 the agent built the state variable, hypotheses and write programs while the operator executed every write. In the agent-controlled Campaign 2 the agent issued instrument commands through a Python wrapper, closed nine propose-preflight-write-read-analyze-decide cycles, self-halted eight of them, rejected two of its own provisional rules by direct measurement, and wrote a mask-defined UTK pattern (letters about 3 µm across) into the measured in-plane superdomain response of a PbZr0.2Ti0.8O3(111) film. Disclosed gates in Campaign 2: the operator supplied the target, stayed present with stop authority, sent 117 prompts over three instrument days, and moved the stage to fresh areas between sessions; an exclusive instrument lock, a file-level stop command and limits on scanner range, bias, footprint and write budget bounded candidate writes. The authors report that six of eight launches failed on faults static checks could have caught and that the function meant to apply all 29 preflight checks was not called on the normal driver path. Code is MIT and the memory files, records and derived data are CC BY 4.0. The 676 raw frames (1.84 GB) and raw session transcripts are not in the repository, and the separate deposit has no DOI or link yet. The acquisition scripts are specific to the Asylum Research/Igor instrument they ran on and are published as a record of what ran; the physical results come from a small number of areas on one film, with retention followed for about an hour.

name: ABLE
domain: Dual-use protein-design tool use by LLM agents
inputs: Self-contained natural-language task prompts with defined tool sets (web search, Biopython, a ProteinMPNN-loaded cloud instance, AlphaFold3 output files) and, where relevant, the correct answers from previous steps
outputs: Per-task scores on a 0-1 scale (algorithmic grading, model-graded rubric for ABLE0), refusal and early-stopping rates, and comparison against a timed human expert baseline
notes: SecureBio benchmark that splits a computational protein-design workflow into nine tasks: one plan-generation task (ABLE0) and eight sequential execution tasks (ABLE1-8) spanning Protein Data Bank structure retrieval and preparation, ProteinMPNN sequence generation and validation of AlphaFold3 outputs, implemented on the UK AI Security Institute's Inspect AI framework. Fifteen frontier models were assessed ten times per task; seven named closed-weight models refused every task. Three tasks (ABLE0, ABLE6, ABLE8) were also run by 11 recruited domain experts with 1, 4 and 2 hours allocated and AI assistants prohibited. For dual-use reasons the authors do not share the full prompts or the ABLE0 rubric and redact the target pathogen, the properties modified and the scoring mechanism, so there is no runnable release and no benchmark artifact to licence (the preprint itself is CC BY 4.0). The single arXiv version (v1, 5 September 2026) carries an author comment that the manuscript was last revised in February 2026, an earlier revision having been presented at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Biosecurity Safeguards for Generative AI. The benchmark measures tool use on a redacted proxy workflow and the authors state it does not include wet-lab validation.

name: NS-Copilot
domain: Neuroscience data analysis with pre-trained neural models (EEG and extracellular spikes)
inputs: Raw neural recordings (NWB, EEGLAB, MATLAB or CSV) and a natural-language analysis task
outputs: Selected pre-trained models, generated analysis code, metrics, per-attempt audit logs and interpretive reports
notes: Multi-agent system from Case Western Reserve University (Planner, Coder, Controller, Interpreter) that chooses among nine integrated EEG and spike models and runs generated code in a Docker sandbox. When no model beats a performance threshold (by default the score of an independent GPT-5.2-Codex run), it replans or patches code for up to two retry rounds. Evaluated on one public dataset each for Alzheimer's EEG, Parkinson's EEG and working-memory spike decoding; the paper reports that forced retries were near-neutral on AD and lowered PD scores, and the system returns the best round. The arXiv record states acceptance to Findings of EMNLP 2026. Code is MIT; integrated model weights keep their own terms (the README lists NDT3 weights as CC-BY-NC-4.0 and REVE weights under a custom licence). Runs need an OpenAI API key, and auto mode also calls the Codex CLI. Closure is computational analysis of supplied data, with no hypothesis generation or wet-lab loop.

name: EvoSCM
domain: Causal-model hypothesis revision through in-silico experimentation (physics, materials, gene-regulatory networks)
inputs: A simulated scientific environment with an experiment interface, observations and configured LLM backends
outputs: Evolved structural causal model hypotheses, an executable law with a natural-language explanation, per-round experiment records and evaluation scores
notes: Method from Sun Yat-sen University and Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School that keeps a population of structural causal model hypotheses, designs discriminative experiments and revises the models when predictions fail. The paper evaluates it on DiscoverPhysics, LLEMA and ActiveSciBench-GRN. The MIT-licensed release builds on the DiscoverPhysics simulator and agent code and covers only the 11 public DiscoverPhysics worlds (N-body backend), not the materials or gene-network adapters. All closure is in silico: simulators, and for materials a pretrained ALIGNN property oracle. Runs need hosted LLM APIs, and explanation scores come from a separate LLM judge. Builds on the DiscoverPhysics benchmark already in the catalog.

name: AgenticAI cross-tissue protein co-abundance pipeline
aliases: Agentic AI uncovers conserved cross-tissue protein co-abundance programs inaccessible to single-dataset analysis
domain: Cross-tissue proteomic co-abundance network comparison and hypothesis generation
inputs: ProteomicsDB tissue iBAQ protein-abundance data, plus UniProt, HPA, hu.MAP 3.0, g:Profiler, STRING, MyGene.info, Open Targets, Europe PMC and web-search lookups
outputs: Tissue co-abundance networks, conserved cross-tissue modules, database annotations and per-tissue-pair markdown research reports
notes: Notebook pipeline by Guan et al. (UIUC School of Information Sciences and University of Michigan; contact Haohan Wang). Four Hugging Face smolagents code agents build tissue co-abundance networks, extract modules conserved across tissue pairs, annotate them from public databases and write research reports. It was applied to all 820 pairs of 41 human tissues and fluids and found 1,833 conserved clusters in 406 pairs. Each agent follows a prescribed step list, and the operator runs the stages cell by cell, choosing tissues or pairs by editing loop filters. The significance tests, figures and published case-study narratives come from the authors' own code and writing. The paper does not evaluate the agents' accuracy. The authors present the agent as an evidence-integration layer, and its mechanistic hypotheses have no wet-lab validation. Running it requires a Hugging Face Inference token (configured for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) and preprocessed data from the authors' Google Drive. Code GPL-3.0.

name: Agentic AFM (EPFL LBNI)
aliases: Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization
domain: Atomic force microscope operation, image-based tuning and post-processing
inputs: Operator-defined imaging intent in natural language, live AFM height, error and KPFM channels, and instrument-control tools exposed over MCP
outputs: Ambiguity-checked instrument commands, bounded imaging-parameter updates, tuned AFM images, post-processed images and session reports
notes: EPFL Laboratory for Bio- and Nano-Instrumentation (Fantner group) framework of three MCP agents: AFM Messenger turns operator instructions into ambiguity-checked commands, AFM Pilot tunes setpoint, integral gain and scan rate from live height and error images, and AFM Doctor post-processes images with pre-approved tools. On a custom open-hardware AFM, AFM Pilot ran iterative acquire-assess-adjust loops on a calibration grating, a butterfly wing and a KPFM sample. In a paired comparison with five human operators from identical detuned starts (setpoint and integral gain only, scored with the agent's AI-vision rubric), both reached the predefined artifact thresholds; with n = 5 the Wilcoxon test cannot reach p < 0.05, so this shows similar outcomes in a small sample. Disclosed gates: humans set the experimental intent and resolve ambiguous commands, approach and scan start need operator confirmation, and tuning stays within operator-set bounds; the authors call it instrument operation, not a self-driving lab. Agent code and benchmark data are promised on publication; the cited repositories were not public on 2026-10-10.

name: SWE-bench Science
domain: Repository-level scientific software engineering by coding agents
inputs: Real scientific-software repositories at fixed baseline commits with issue-driven, expert-exploratory or engineering-integration task instructions and public tests
outputs: Agent patches applied in a separate clean verifier container (rebuilt for compiled projects) and scored by held-out private tests: public and private scores, Fail2Pass, Pass2Pass and binary pass@1
notes: Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University (OpenMOSS) benchmark of 119 tasks from 98 GitHub repositories across 20 scientific domains; the best reported agent, Claude Code with Opus-5 (max), reaches 47.90% pass@1. Project tooling is MIT; task sources, instructions and image contents keep their upstream licences. Per-task environment and verifier images (with held-out tests and graders) are public on Docker Hub, and runs use the third-party Pier runner. 23 tasks with GPL-family, non-commercial or restricted-material upstream terms are excluded unless explicitly opted in. It measures repository-level repair and integration of scientific code, not end-to-end research, and is distinct from SciCode.

access_evidence.software_license: MIT (root LICENSE, OpenMOSS (SII)) for project-owned tooling and documentation; HF dataset card tagged MIT. Per NOTICE.md, upstream-derived task metadata, instructions, source snapshots and image contents keep upstream licences; held-out tests and graders ship in public Docker Hub verifier images without a separately stated licence. 23 opt-in tasks are GPL-family (18), non-commercial (2) or restricted-material (3).

name: GoalEvolve
domain: Electronic design automation: goal-driven evolution of OpenROAD physical-design algorithms
inputs: OpenROAD source snapshot, design and technology inputs, a frozen multi-objective QoR target region and a bounded editable source scope
outputs: Evolved OpenROAD C++ source variants with full-flow post-route QoR records, validity checks and mechanism evidence
notes: Fudan University system for evolving chip physical-design algorithms. Given a frozen multi-objective QoR target, the framework converts unmet targets into normalized gaps and uses stage-resolved checkpoint evidence to locate the bottleneck stage; an LLM Teacher then narrows the search to an algorithmic decision and source region, and parallel Codex-based Student agents edit, build and evaluate bounded OpenROAD C++ changes through a checkpointed post-placement optimization and global-routing flow. Reported on eight ASAP7 designs against default OpenROAD and commercial-tool targets; closure is computational only, and humans fix the goal contract, editable source scope and evaluation flow. The BSD-3-Clause repository includes replay artifacts for the eight evolved sources, while new campaigns need the Codex CLI and a model-provider API key. The domain is engineering algorithm discovery for chip physical design.

name: The Little Scientist
domain: Hypothesis-driven algorithm discovery on computational-biology benchmarks (protein fitness prediction, DNA motif discovery)
inputs: A benchmark with an automated evaluator returning per-instance diagnostics, a problem description and function signature, and optional human-supplied input data
outputs: Iterated scoring algorithms with logged hypotheses, predictions and evaluation history; final algorithms such as the Delta V ensemble strategy and the DALE motif finder
notes: Single-author framework (Travis Smith), called SEF (Scientific Experiment Framework) in the delta-v repository. A Scientist agent cycles through hypothesis, prediction, implementation, benchmark evaluation and reconciliation; a Kuhn agent injects a paradigm-shifting conjecture paired with a cross-disciplinary inspiration when progress plateaus. Agents run via cron on the OpenClaw platform with GLM-4.7. Reported outputs are Delta V, which the paper ranks first on the ProteinGym DMS substitutions zero-shot leaderboard (self-reported; the leaderboard pull request was still open and unmerged on 2026-10-10), and DALE, a DNA motif finder with higher mean AUROC than STREME across 132 ENCODE ChIP-seq datasets (0.842 vs 0.803); the agent wrote DALE in Python and the best version was ported to C for the benchmark. Closure is computational only. The human designed the evaluation infrastructure, rebuilt it after the first motif search stalled, supplied the five-model predictions behind the largest ProteinGym gain, and can trigger Kuhn cycles; the repository setup guide says the Scientist-to-Kuhn handoff is run manually or by a main OpenClaw agent. Both repositories are Apache-2.0. Orchestration scripts and Scientist/Kuhn prompts are released only for the ProteinGym case, in little-scientist-delta-v. The paper's code statement points the framework to little-scientist-dale, which holds only the motif agent prompt and best strategy, and the archived search history the paper places in delta-v is not in that repository.

name: AutoResearchEval
domain: Process-level failure diagnosis of end-to-end autonomous research agents across seven scientific domains
inputs: Research queries derived from published papers (premise and open tension, with the paper's key claims and conclusion withheld), plus agent trajectories and produced artifacts for judging
outputs: Failure labels under the 45-pattern AutoResearch Failure Taxonomy (ARFT), per-stage judge analyses, and optimization scores against source-paper results
notes: Built by Prentis AI (author affiliations also include Stanford University and Titan Holdings): 100 tasks from published papers in chemistry, geophysics, materials science, physics, scientific computing, biology and medicine. 70 are open-ended discovery tasks from 2024-onward papers; 30 are target-anchored optimization tasks that follow NatureBench's task selection. The CC BY 4.0 Hugging Face dataset holds the task files and 800 agent trajectories with per-rollout outcome metadata from eight harness-model pairs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI). Per-trajectory ARFT labels are not in the dataset, although the paper states that annotations are released. The artifact-aware judge is MIT-licensed and on PyPI as autoresearcheval; its first stage needs an authenticated Claude Code CLI. The rest of the GitHub code has no licence file. The container rollout environment, including the held-out data and evaluation service for the optimization tasks, is not released. Judge agreement is reported only in aggregate over 50 calibration trajectories. This is a different resource from AutoResearchBench and EvoMap AutoResearch.

name: VALG
domain: Machine-learning theory: theorem formulation and graph-structured proof development
inputs: An ML-theory research direction or open problem, with an optional research brief
outputs: Literature surveys, perspective branches, theorem contracts, reviewed proof graphs and LaTeX theorem-candidate reports
notes: University of Hong Kong system released as an MIT-licensed bundle of 17 Codex skills (a controller, stage skills and shared templates) that runs inside Codex with subagents, without a standalone runtime; the archived runs used gpt-5.6-sol. Separate reviewer subagents diagnose failed proofs, and the controller routes each failure to derivation, proof-structure or theorem-formulation repair; formulation failures produce explicitly related variants or relaxations. On nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems, two runs reached internally finalized candidates matching the source scope; checking was by LLM reviewers plus a rough human audit, without formal verification. Disclosed gate: the default interactive mode places a human-expert checkpoint after each pre-proof stage, and the archived run logs record such checkpoint decisions; autopilot approves by default and was used for the later stages of one run.

name: Periodic Neon (Periodic Labs)
domain: Agentic powder X-ray diffraction phase analysis in materials-synthesis labs searching for superconductors and magnets
inputs: Powder XRD patterns with synthesis context such as precursors, conditions and related experiments
outputs: XRD phase analyses of multiphase samples (which phases formed and in what proportions) with reasoning over competing phase hypotheses
notes: Periodic Labs midtrained the open-weight, trillion-parameter Kimi K2.6 on a blend of academic literature, code and experimental data, then applied reinforcement learning on its own lab data. The resulting model, Periodic Neon, runs in the Periodic Harness, which provides laboratory context, in-house structure and simulation databases and XRD analysis software. The company reports that Neon is deployed in its high-throughput labs to analyse XRD results. Its reported 55.3% success on the internal 134-sample FrontierXRD set is scored by an LLM-judge ensemble calibrated against expert ratings. Evidence is company posts only, with no paper, and no public release of the model, harness or benchmark was found. The September 2026 posts present AI direction of campaigns, synthesis and experiment choice as work being extended, and they demonstrate no AI-directed physical loop.

name: FARS
inputs: Seed AI/ML research directions (nine in the public deployment); no interactive user input during execution
outputs: Hypotheses, plans, code, experiment logs, results and complete short papers, with per-project artifacts committed to GitLab
notes: Built by Analemma. Stage-specific agents for ideation, planning, experimentation and writing share a workspace and run each project without human intervention during execution. The first public deployment ran 417 hours on a 160-GPU cluster from nine seeded directions and produced 166 papers across 67 AI/ML topics. Before arXiv submission, a small selected subset got a minimal human integrity review that left the research content unchanged. Volunteer reviews (282 reviews of 140 papers) found review-worthy outputs alongside recurring narrow scope, methodological limits and integrity issues. The system code is not released, and the analemma.ai platform was unreachable in checks on 2026-08-13 and 2026-10-10. All 166 deployment papers, with human and LLM reviews, are on Hugging Face under Apache-2.0. Per-project artifacts are public on GitLab, without a licence.

name: SFitterAgents
domain: LHC analysis re-casting and global SMEFT fits (particle physics)
inputs: A published LHC measurement (arXiv paper or HEPData record) and the SMEFT operators of interest
outputs: Reviewed measurement extractions, MadGraph SM and SMEFT predictions, validated SFitter datacards, global-fit intervals and provenance records
notes: Built at Universität Heidelberg (Diefenbacher, Plehn, Schiller, Schmal) on top of MadGraphTeam's MadAgents (v3); the repository bundles the SFitter fitting code with a Claude Code multi-agent system. In the paper the agents proposed, re-simulated and fitted an ATLAS differential ttZ measurement into the top-sector global SMEFT analysis, with every step supervised by a physicist; closure is computational only. MIT licence; third-party components keep their own terms. Running it needs the Claude Code CLI with a Claude subscription or API credits, Apptainer, and a SLURM cluster with GPU nodes for real re-interpretations.

name: LAMMPS-Agents
aliases: Multi-Agentic AI Framework for End-to-End Atomistic Simulations
domain: Natural-language-driven LAMMPS atomistic simulation of materials properties
inputs: Natural-language materials-property request; OpenAI API key; local (or configured HPC) LAMMPS installation
outputs: Atomic structures, reviewed LAMMPS inputs, executed simulations and analysed properties (lattice and elastic constants, phonon dispersion, melting point) with vision-model checks of OVITO renderings
notes: AutoGen multi-agent framework from Argonne National Laboratory (Center for Nanoscale Materials and ALCF) with UIC. Specialised agents build structures, find interatomic potentials (with a web-surfer agent), write and review LAMMPS inputs, run simulations and analyse results; the analysis agent uses a vision model to check OVITO renderings and plots. The shipped code runs LAMMPS locally; an HPC module for Argonne's cluster is included but mostly disabled. Published in Digital Discovery (2026). The MIT-licensed GitHub repository, maintained by first author Katerina Vriza, is linked from the authors' Zenodo code record; agent chat logs and human-expert comparison runs are on Zenodo. Closure is computational only: the public code asks a human for input at every turn of the LAMMPS input-creator agent and ships a memory built from human teachings. Autonomy is rated from code and abstract because the article page was not machine-readable.

name: Finch
domain: Notebook-based analysis of biological experimental and omics data
inputs: Dataset(s) plus a natural-language research question or requested analysis
outputs: Executed Jupyter notebook (Python, R or Bash) with analyses, figures and a final answer
notes: FutureHouse data-analysis agent built on Aviary that iteratively writes and runs Jupyter-notebook code. It generated the BixBench agent trajectories and is the data-analysis component of Robin, which can launch ten independent Finch trajectories on wet-lab data. The public repository (formerly data-analysis-crow) is Apache-2.0, with releases v1.0.0 and v1.5.0 (September 2025). Edison Scientific hosts it as the Analysis agent (client alias JobNames.FINCH); the hosted version is documented with extra protein and figure tools and may differ from the public code. Closure is computational; experiments and data upload stay with the scientist.
